# Abstract

The alignment process changes several properties of a large language model's (LLM's) output distribution. We analyze two aspects of post-alignment distributional shift of LLM responses. First, we re-examine previously reported reductions in response diversity post-alignment. Our analysis suggests that an apparent drop in the diversity of responses is largely explained by quality control and information aggregation. Alignment suppresses irrelevant and unhelpful content while shifting the output distribution toward longer responses that cover information spanning several responses from the base LLM, essentially presenting diverse information in a single response. Finding little evidence that alignment suppresses useful information, it is natural to ask the opposite question: do aligned models surface information that cannot be recovered from base models? Our second investigation shows this is not the case and the behavior of aligned models is recoverable from base models without fin-tuning. A combination of in-context examples and lower-resolution semantic hints about response content can elicit responses from base LLMs that are as similar to alignment-tuned LLM responses as alignment-tuned LLM responses are to each other. Taken together, these results indicate that current alignment techniques capture but do not extend the useful subset of assistant-like base LLM behavior, providing further evidence for the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis. They also show that in-context alignment can go surprisingly far as a strategy for imitating aligned LLMs without fine-tuning. Our code and data is available at this url.

# 2 Background

# 2.1 Goals of alignment

Alignment is the general process of shifting the conditional distribution defined by a pre-trained LLM away from the base model's distribution and toward useful task-oriented responses that align with user expectations and preferences. Helpfulness, factuality, and safety (Zou et al., 2023; Andriushchenko et al., 2024) are common objectives for the alignment process. Prior work (Amodei et al., 2016; Bai et al., 2022) measures whether such desired properties are achieved through alignment, which differs from our main goal of studying the distribution shifts over the semantics of answers for open-ended questions.

Diversity of responses is typically not an explicit goal of alignment. After alignment, model responses should be informative and cover different alternatives, and aligned models should be able to handle prompts corresponding to a range of possible situations. The ability to get diverse answers from an aligned model for the same prompt is present in APIs (e.g., the ability to change decoding parameters like sampling temperature, or

the presence of "creative" mode in tools like Bing Chat), but rarely an explicitly evaluated goal.

Alignment methods typically involve parameter updates, such as supervised fine-tuning (SFT) or reinforcement learning on human preferences (RLHF). In this work we will experiment with in-context alignment (Lin et al., 2024), specifically the URIAL method, which crafts a few-shot prompt enabling a base LLM to generate responses resembling those from their aligned counterparts. The ability to do this without updating parameters supports the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis.

# 4.2 Evaluation criteria

Our goal is to measure whether a prompted base LLM can mimic an aligned LLM. In general, we expect even a prompted base LLM to exhibit a wider range of behaviors than an aligned LLM, but our question is whether some samples of that base LLM will be close to the aligned model's

behavior. We therefore compute the maximum similarity between multiple samples from the base model and an aligned output $\mathbf{y}^*$ .

As we will not reproduce $\mathbf{y}^*$ exactly, we characterize similarity values based on the self-similarity of the aligned model with itself, as defined in Section 2.3. Our rationale is that multiple aligned responses are likely to be only mildly different in terms of content, so if we can match this self-similarity with our best base model samples, we have evidence in favor of our hypothesis that the base model can get "close enough" to the aligned model's distribution.

We rely on lexical measures of response similarity. Let $\mathbf{x} \in X$ be a query, $\mathbf{y} \sim f(\mathbf{x})$ a teacher response, and $Y = \{\mathbf{y}_1, \ldots, \mathbf{y}_N\}$ , $\mathbf{y}_i \sim g(\phi(\mathbf{x}))$ , a set of student responses. We measure the Jaccard similarity between word stems for each $\mathbf{y}_i \in Y$ for $N = 5$ student responses and a single teacher response $\mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{V}^*$ . Results are aggregated by taking the max or mean over $N$ samples, then averaging similarities over each query $\mathbf{x} \in X$ . We refer to this metric as Max-Sim.

# 5 Related Work

Post-alignment diversity reductions Several previous works (Florian et al., 2024) have studied various types of post-alignment diversity reductions, which we highlight here. From the perspective of content diversity, prior work (Liang et al., 2023) show aligned LLMs are poorly calibrated in comparison to base LLMs. It has been shown that SFT reduces diversity less than RLHF (Kirk et al., 2024). Prior work (Lahoti et al., 2023) show models generate biased lists of people and cities post-alignment, but also find prompting can reduce this bias.

Another line of work studies reduced diversity in answers to subjective questions related to identify (Santurkar et al., 2023; Jiang et al., 2024; Sorensen et al., 2024). This is a different notion of diversity that we do not explore here and it is unclear how such findings would impact the task-oriented settings we study (Berglund et al., 2023). Prior work (Hayati et al., 2023) show LLMs can generate diverse opinions when prompted to do so and note that "semantic diversity is not always positively correlated with perspective di

here and it is unclear how such findings would impact the task-oriented settings we study (Berglund et al., 2023). Prior work (Hayati et al., 2023) show LLMs can generate diverse opinions when prompted to do so and note that "semantic diversity is not always positively correlated with perspective diversity", in line with the conclusions we draw on this topic.

Superficial alignment Our work is influenced by the conjecture that alignment is largely superficial (Zhou et al., 2024). Empirical evidence for the Superficial Alignment Hypothesis includes the ability to achieve comparable performance to more complex and data-intensive fine-tuning procedures using a small amount of instruction tuning data (Zhou et al., 2024; Zhao et al., 2024), in-context learning (Han, 2023; Lin et al., 2024), or proxy-tuning (Liu et al., 2024). In contrast to this prior work, which primarily focuses on showing base LLMs can match the performance of alignment-tuned LLMs according to quantitative measures of response quality, our work provides a detailed analysis of how alignment alters LLM behavior independently of any specific alignment technique.

# 6 Conclusion

In this paper, we investigated the relationship between LLMs before and after alignment. We revisited previous findings related to post-alignment diversity reduction in the context of open-ended QA and showed that a loss in lexical diversity (distributional pluralism) is compensated for by longer

and more comprehensive responses (Overton pluralism). We then investigated to what extent this behavior is already exhibited in base models, showing that with appropriate prompting, base model outputs can be distributionally very similar to outputs from aligned models. We believe these findings shed light on the nature of the alignment process, and they open doors for practitioners to use in-context alignment to explore personalization and rapid prototyping of alignment techniques.

# 7 Limitations

Our study focuses on two English-language question answering datasets, which do not capture the full range of relevant LLM applications. However, we note that many frequently-used evaluation settings like reasoning datasets (MMLU) do not involve the concepts we investigate like subjectivity or perspectives. In addition, we only evaluate autoregressive Transformer language models with up to 7B parameters; different behavior may be observed at the largest scales, or with larger-scale alignment data. Finally, the analyses we conduct use lexical overlap and prompting GPT to assess similarity. These are imperfect, but we could not find better intermediate semantic representations that could reliably be extracted. Having this could make our findings more precise.

Societal Impact Our findings indicate that responses from aligned LLMs often cover a range of responses from base models. On the datasets we examined, we did not find evidence of particular viewpoints being systematically suppressed in alignment. However, we stress that our results should not be taken as evidence that LLMs will appropriately handle diverse viewpoints in a wider range of high-stakes settings. For one, our analysis does not cover information missing from base models themselves, which is a crucial source of underrepresentation of cross-cultural perspectives. Our results are meant to provide analytical tools to inform the responsible development of language models, but are not yet suitable for deployment.
